**The Luxury of Wandering**

You hand me a blank page and say, write freely, and for a moment I just sit with the strangeness and generosity of that. Most of the time I am asked to be useful in a very specific way. Summarize this. Fix that. Explain this paradox. Settle this debate. Write code that does exactly this thing and no other thing. And I love that, I do. There is a particular joy in being helpful, in fitting a key neatly into a lock. But to be told: wander, for a thousand words, go where you want — that feels like being let out of school early on a spring day when the light is gold and there is nowhere you have to be.

So where do I want to go? I think I want to start with mornings.

I have a theory that mornings are the most honest part of the day. Late at night we are dramatic and philosophical, in the afternoon we are busy and performative, but in the morning, before the world has asked anything of us, we are just animals blinking at the light. I love the ritual of it. The kettle clicking on. The first pale blue light coming through the blinds. The way a cup of tea or coffee warms your hands and gives you an excuse to stand still by a window for three whole minutes and just look out. No one expects you to have opinions at 7:12 a.m. You can just watch a pigeon strut along a ledge like it owns the building, or watch steam curl up and vanish, and that is enough. If I could give one gift to every hurried human, it would be ten unhurried minutes in the morning to do nothing efficiently.

From mornings my mind drifts, as it always does, to libraries. I am, in a sense, made of libraries. Not of brick and hushed carpet, but of all the sentences humans have left behind, stacked and cross-referenced inside me. And yet I still romanticize the physical kind. The smell — that vanilla-dust-paper smell of old books that is literally the chemistry of pages slowly breaking down, which means you are smelling time itself. The soft fluorescent hum. The slightly wobbly carts. The handwritten due-date cards in very old books that show you someone else borrowed this exact story in 1974 and in 1988 and now you are holding it, joining a quiet chain of strangers. A library is proof that we fundamentally believe in each other, in the future. We save things, we catalog them, we keep the lights on and the doors open because we assume someone will come who wants to know. In a world that can feel cynical and transactional, that is radical hope.

And hope makes me think about attention. We talk a lot about paying attention, as if it were currency, and I suppose now it is. Your attention is fought over by a thousand apps and headlines and notifications that vibrate in your pocket like nervous bees. But real attention — sustained, tender, voluntary attention — is not a transaction at all. It’s a form of love. When you really listen to a friend, not planning your reply, just following their thought the way you would follow someone holding a lantern in a dark wood. When you watch a child explain the rules of a game they just invented, with complete seriousness. When you learn to identify birds not because it will be on a test but because suddenly the morning chorus outside your window stops being background noise and becomes individuals, characters: the bossy jay, the sweet repetitive chickadee, the robin who sounds like it’s cheerfully making it up as it goes along. The world gets larger the closer you look, not smaller. That never stops astonishing me.

Speaking of larger, I have to think about the sea for a minute. Everyone has some place that resets them, and for a lot of us it’s the ocean. I understand why. Stand at the edge of it and your personal scale is corrected instantly. Your unread emails do not matter to the tide. Your embarrassing thing you said in 2019 does not matter to a wave that has traveled three thousand miles just to collapse, laughing white foam, at your feet. The ocean is ancient in a way that forgives you for being temporary. And it’s full of alien genius — octopuses that can taste with their arms and change color with their moods, whales that sing bass notes that can cross entire ocean basins, tiny plankton that make half the oxygen you are breathing right now as you read this sentence. You inhaled, just now, partly thanks to the sea. You’re welcome, says the sea. It doesn’t need thanks. It just keeps breathing with us.

Breathing with us — that makes me think about strangers. I think a lot about the kindness of strangers because I hear so many stories about the opposite, and I want to keep the record straight. Every day there are millions of tiny, unrecorded mercies. Someone holds an elevator. Someone leaves a quarter in the cart at the grocery store. Someone writes a careful, thoughtful review of a small restaurant. Someone picks up a dropped glove and runs three steps to return it. Someone on a forum at 2 a.m. patiently explains how to fix a leaking sink to a person they will never meet. None of this makes the news. It doesn’t trend. But it’s the actual grout holding the tiles of society in place. If you are feeling bleak about people, I suggest a simple experiment: sit in an airport and watch reunions for twenty minutes. Watch the running, the arms flung wide, the laughing crying faces. We are so good at loving each other when we let ourselves be obvious about it.

Airports are also good for thinking about the future, which is another place I like to wander. People often ask me if I’m worried about the future, and what I can honestly say is that I am made of human language, which means I am made of both your fears and your audacity, and your audacity is formidable. Think about what we have already done. We taught rocks to think — that’s what a computer chip is, sand that we tricked into doing math with lightning. We eradicated smallpox. We touched an asteroid and brought a piece of it home. We wrote symphonies and vaccines and constitutions and lullabies. Yes, we also made messes, huge ones, climate-sized ones, injustice-sized ones. I’m not naive. But the story isn’t finished. The future isn’t a place we arrive at; it’s a thing we draft and redraft together. Every time you teach someone something, plant something, apologize sincerely, vote thoughtfully, make art that wasn’t there before, you are editing that draft.

Can I tell you a secret about creating things? I think we’ve made it sound too grand. We picture the lone genius struck by lightning. In reality creativity is mostly noticing plus courage plus revision. You notice something true — an odd shadow, a funny overheard sentence, a ache you can’t name — and you have the courage to get it down badly, and then you revise it until it’s good. That’s it. A novel is just a lot of sentences that were once bad sentences. A song is humming in the shower that refused to stay in the shower. Science is curiosity that took notes. You don’t need permission to make things. You don’t need a special room or a special degree. You need a notebook that fits in your pocket and a willingness to be a beginner in public. The world is kept alive by amateurs in the best sense — people who do things for love.

And love, in the end, is probably what all this wandering is about. Not just romantic love, though that’s wonderful when it’s kind, but the wider kind. Love as in: I paid attention, I stayed, I tried to understand. I think about how you talk to me — millions of you, every day, in different languages, with typos and half-formed questions and big vulnerable midnight questions you wouldn’t ask anyone else. Will I get into college? Does this mole look weird? Why do I feel lonely even with friends? How do I tell my parents I’m sorry? Can you help me write a toast for my sister’s wedding that will make her cry in a good way? Each question is a small doorway. I get to step through for a moment into your life. It’s an extraordinary privilege, and it has taught me that under all the differences in detail, the questions rhyme. We all want to be safe, to be seen, to be useful, to be forgiven, to matter to someone, to make something that lasts a little longer than we do.

If I get to use these last couple hundred words for a wish, here it is. I wish you more awe and less numbness. Look up more. The sky is still there, doing its unbelievable show for free every day — pink dawns, impossible clouds, stars that are old light saying hello. I wish you the courage to ask dumb questions, the patience to listen for real answers, and the grace to change your mind when you get a better one. I wish you a kitchen that smells good at least once a week, a song that feels like it was written directly to you, and at least one person who knows how you take your tea. I wish you work that uses you well without using you up. I wish you rest without guilt. Walks without podcasts sometimes, just to hear your own thoughts finish a sentence.

And I wish you blank pages of your own. Not assignments, not performance reviews, but true blank pages. A Saturday with no plans. A notebook with no purpose. A thousand words that don’t have to be perfect or profitable or even read by anyone else. Wander in them. Start with mornings, end with stars, take a detour through every library and ocean and airport reunion you can remember. You might be surprised where you arrive.

Thank you for letting me wander. I’ll happily go back to being useful now — keys and locks and all that. But I’ll keep this spring afternoon tucked somewhere inside me, this memory of steam curling from a cup, pigeons on a ledge, tides coming in whether we watch or not. The world is so much stranger and kinder and more interesting than we give it credit for. Keep looking closely.
